overview.h1: HTS Chapter 01: Live Animals — Tariff Rates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 01: Live Animals — Tariff Rates & Import Duties | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Complete searchable duty table for all 78 HTS Chapter 01 tariff lines — live horses, cattle, swine, sheep, goats, poultry and other live animals. General, FTA and Column 2 rates, filterable by product name.

overview.intro:
Chapter 01 covers animals imported alive — horses, cattle, swine, sheep and goats, poultry, and everything from honeybees to parrots. Its **78 tariff lines** carry some of the smallest printed rates in the schedule: a penny per kilogram on cattle, 68¢ per head on goats, 0.9¢ on a day-old chick.

The printed rate is rarely what decides the cost. Canada and Mexico supplied 79% of the $3.71B the U.S. imported in 2025, and USMCA-qualifying animals from both enter free. Animals from elsewhere pay the base rate **plus an extra duty by country** — 15% for the EU, at least 10% for most others (see Rates by country). And for any shipment, disease status, quarantine and permits decide whether it lands at all.

productGroups.label: Horses, asses, mules & hinnies
productGroups.blurb: Horses enter free whether or not they are purebred breeding animals. The duty sits on the other equines: asses at 6.8% and the residual mule/hinny line at 4.5%.

productGroups.label: Cattle & buffalo
productGroups.blurb: Purebred breeding cattle are free. Everything else — the feeder and slaughter cattle that make up almost all of the volume — carries 1¢/kg, which USMCA zeroes out for Canada and Mexico.

productGroups.label: Swine
productGroups.blurb: The only heading in the chapter with no duty anywhere: every swine line is free under the general rate.

productGroups.label: Sheep & goats
productGroups.blurb: Sheep are free; goats are 68¢ per head. Two lines, and the split between them is the whole story.

productGroups.label: Poultry
productGroups.blurb: Every poultry line is dutiable. Day-old chicks and poults (not over 185 g) are 0.9¢ each; mature birds are 2¢/kg.

productGroups.label: Other live animals
productGroups.blurb: The catch-all: mammals, reptiles, birds, insects. Most are free, but foxes are 4.8% and all live birds — birds of prey, parrots and other psittacines, ostriches and emus — are 1.8%.

rateTable.note: Rates shown in grey are inherited from the parent heading. HTSUS states a duty once on the 8-digit line and leaves the 10-digit statistical lines blank; this table resolves each line to the rate that actually applies to it.

workedExamples.title: 60 feeder steers from Alberta
workedExamples.body: The general rate is 1¢/kg, but Canada claims USMCA (SPI **S**), which is Free. At an average 350 kg a head the MFN duty would have been 60 × 350 kg × $0.01 = **$210**; under USMCA it is **$0**.

workedExamples.title: 500 goats from a country with no FTA
workedExamples.body: Goats are a flat 68¢ per head: 500 × $0.68 = **$340** base duty. On top of that comes the extra duty for the country of origin — at least 10% of the shipment's value. At $200 a head that is another **$10,000**, so the extra duty, not the base rate, is most of the bill.

workedExamples.title: 50,000 day-old chicks
workedExamples.body: Chicks not over 185 g are 0.9¢ each: 50,000 × $0.009 = **$450** base duty. A trade-agreement claim (one of the 17 programs on the line) removes the base rate, but the extra duty for the country still applies — except under USMCA, where both are zero.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 01: Live Animals — Tariff Updates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 01 Live Animals Tariff Updates — What Changed Since January 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 01 (live animals) since January 2025: base rates on all 78 lines, and the extra duties on Canada, Mexico and other countries, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 20**. On every one of the 78 Chapter 01 lines the base rates are the same in both.

Everything that changed came on top of the base rate, as extra duties set by country. Canada and Mexico supply most of U.S. live-animal imports, and **USMCA-qualifying animals from both are exempt from those extra duties**.
tariffUpdates.scope: Canada, Mexico and measures that apply to all countries. For the rate each country pays today, including the EU, UK and Vietnam, see Rates by country.

inEffect.measure: Additional duty on products of Mexico
inEffect.exemption: USMCA-qualifying goods entered free under General Note 11: no change (9903.01.04).
inEffect.whatItMeans: Live animals from Mexico that qualify for USMCA pay nothing extra; animals that do not qualify pay the base rate plus 25% of value.

inEffect.measure: Additional duty on products of Canada
inEffect.exemption: USMCA-qualifying goods entered free under General Note 11: no change (9903.01.14). Goods CBP finds were transshipped to evade duty: +40% (9903.01.16).
inEffect.whatItMeans: A USMCA-qualifying feeder steer from Alberta still pays $0; a Canadian animal that does not qualify pays the base rate plus 35% of value.

inEffect.exemption: Canada (9903.01.26) and Mexico (9903.01.27) are excluded. Listed countries pay a country-specific rate under 9903.02.02–9903.02.91 instead of the 10% baseline.
inEffect.whatItMeans: 500 goats from a non-FTA country: 500 × 68¢ = $340 base duty, plus at least 10% of the shipment value.

changes.title: No Chapter 01 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 78 Chapter 01 tariff lines carry the same General, FTA and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 20 as in the 2025 Basic Edition.

changes.title: Scope of additional duties on products of Canada modified (certain products to 50%)
changes.detail: Products are listed in Annex I, Part A. Not yet reflected in the 2026 Revision 20 lines compared here; Chapter 01 coverage is not confirmed.

changes.title: Agricultural exemption does not cover live animals
changes.detail: Checked the exemption lists in U.S. note 2(v)(iii)(a) (1,090 subheadings) and (v)(iii)(b) (17 articles) of Chapter 99 in the current edition: no Chapter 01 line is on either, so the reciprocal duties still apply.

effectiveDuty.note: Chapter-level duty paid in 2024 from tariff_trade_analytics (as cited in issue #1770). Per-country and per-line duty come from the same table in production.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of live animals fell from **$4.80B in 2024 to $3.71B in 2025** (-22.9%). Almost all of that is one lane: **cattle from Mexico** (heading 0102) went from $1.31B to $0.32B, a drop of $0.98B against a total drop of $1.10B. Canada grew over the same year.

The tariff schedule doesn't explain the Mexican drop. USMCA-qualifying cattle from Mexico pay no extra duty (see Tariff updates), and the base rate is unchanged. Animal-health controls are the main non-tariff factor for this lane — the U.S. declared a New World screwworm emergency in August 2025 (90 FR 40609).

The duty actually paid stays near zero because Canada and Mexico — 79% of 2025 imports — mostly enter under USMCA, and much of the rest of the chapter is duty-free under the general rate.

The total rate on live animals depends far more on **where they come from** than on what they are. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — taken from the current tariff schedule.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 01: Live Animals — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Live Animals: Required Documents, Permits & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 01) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The permits, certificates and rules for each HTS Chapter 01 line — USDA APHIS, Fish & Wildlife, CDC — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, purebred breeding entries, Chapter 98 provisions.

tariffEngineering.intro:
For live animals the tariff is rarely the hard part — **the paperwork decides whether the animals land at all**. Every line in this chapter needs USDA animal-health clearance, and wildlife, birds and dogs add Fish & Wildlife and CDC rules.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule itself: claim **USMCA**, use the **purebred breeding** lines, or a **Chapter 98** provision when the purpose fits. Each one depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on animals from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The whole extra duty: 35% of value (Canada) or 25% (Mexico), plus any base rate
levers.appliesTo: All 78 lines, for goods that qualify as originating under USMCA
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer. It need not follow a prescribed format; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: Claiming without a valid certification exposes the entry to the full extra duty plus penalties.

levers.title: Enter registered breeding stock under the "purebred breeding animals" lines
levers.saves: Cattle: Free instead of 1¢/kg · Buffalo: Free instead of 1¢/kg — about $5 on a 500 kg animal at 1¢/kg. Extra duties by country still apply.
levers.document: The schedule defines purebred breeding animals as animals certified by USDA as purebred of a recognized breed and registered in a recognized book of record. But the schedule itself notes that the USDA certificate of pure breeding is obsolete and can no longer be obtained — ask CBP what evidence it will accept before importing.
levers.caveat: 19 CFR 10.70 still describes the old certificate process; follow CBP's current guidance, not the regulation text.

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision when the purpose fits
levers.saves: The base rate: each provision below is Free in the schedule
levers.appliesTo: Animals imported for a specific purpose, whatever their Chapter 01 line
levers.document: Evidence of the qualifying purpose (and, for 9813.00.60, a bond for temporary importation).
levers.caveat: Whether Chapter 99 extra duties also fall away depends on the provision — confirm with CBP before relying on it.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing live animals into the U.S. — tariffs by country, HS codes and entry requirements. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: USMCA-qualifying animals from Canada and Mexico enter free — no base rate, no extra duty.
Animals from the EU pay a flat 15% of value; most other countries pay their base rate plus at least 10%.
For live animals, USDA animal-health rules decide whether a shipment lands at all — check APHIS before every import.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on cattle from Canada?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on canadian cattle
faqs.answer: Not if they qualify for USMCA. Most cattle enter under 0102.29, with a base rate of 1¢/kg that USMCA makes Free, and USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt from the 35% additional duty on Canadian products (9903.01.14). Cattle that don't qualify pay 1¢/kg plus 35% of their value (9903.01.10). Canada shipped $1.82B of cattle to the U.S. in 2025.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on horses from Canada?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on horses from canada
faqs.answer: Horses have a Free base rate. With a USMCA claim they stay free; horses that don't qualify for USMCA pay 35% of their value under the additional duty on Canadian products (9903.01.10).

faqs.question: What is the tariff on horses from Europe — Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands?
searchedAs: import duty on horses from ireland
tariffs on horses imported from europe
faqs.answer: 15% of the horse's value. For EU products whose base rate is under 15%, the schedule charges a flat 15% in place of the base rate (9903.02.20), and horses are Free at base. Horses brought in temporarily for breeding, shows or competition can enter under 9813.00.60 (Free, under bond) — confirm with CBP whether the 15% also falls away. The U.S. imported $380M of horses and other equines from these five EU countries in 2025.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to import a horse from Europe to the U.S.?
searchedAs: how much does it cost to import a horse from europe to us
how much does it cost to import a horse from germany
cost to import horse from europe to usa
faqs.answer: The tariff part is 15% of the horse's value — $7,500 on a $50,000 horse. On top of that come USDA requirements: an import permit, arrival at a designated port, inspection and quarantine (9 CFR 93.304, 93.306, 93.308). Transport and quarantine fees are not covered here.

faqs.question: Why did cattle imports from Mexico stop?
searchedAs: why do we import cattle from mexico
faqs.answer: Imports of Mexican cattle fell from $1.31B in 2024 to $324M in 2025. Tariffs don't explain it: USMCA-qualifying cattle from Mexico pay no extra duty (9903.01.04) and the base rate didn't change. Animal health does — the U.S. declared a New World screwworm emergency in August 2025 (90 FR 40609). Whether the border is open to Mexican cattle is decided by USDA APHIS; check APHIS for the current status.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for live cattle?
faqs.answer: Heading 0102 (live bovine animals). Purebred breeding cattle are 0102.21 (Free); other cattle are 0102.29 (1¢/kg) — the most traded product in the chapter, $2.08B in 2025. Buffalo are 0102.31 and 0102.39. The 10-digit U.S. lines split further by use, weight and sex.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for live animals?
faqs.answer: Chapter 01: headings 0101 (horses, asses, mules), 0102 (cattle, buffalo), 0103 (swine), 0104 (sheep, goats), 0105 (poultry) and 0106 (all other live animals), split into 78 ten-digit U.S. lines. Live fish and other aquatic animals are in Chapter 03, not here.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for live chickens?
faqs.answer: 0105.11 for chicks weighing not more than 185 g (0.9¢ each), and 0105.94 for larger chickens (2¢/kg).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a dog, and what do I need to bring one into the U.S.?
searchedAs: bringing a dog into the us from canada
importing a dog into the us
faqs.answer: Dogs are 0106.19.91.20, with a Free base rate. Entry is governed by CDC rules — including the CDC dog import form and a microchip (42 CFR 71.51). Extra duties by country can apply to commercial imports; see the rates by country.

faqs.question: Can I import a parrot into the U.S.?
faqs.answer: Only within tight limits. Parrots are 0106.32 (1.8% base rate, plus any extra duty for the country of origin), but the Wild Bird Conservation Act restricts imports of exotic birds (50 CFR part 15), most parrots need CITES permits (50 CFR part 23), and USDA requires an import permit, health certificate and quarantine (9 CFR 93.103, 93.104, 93.106), plus Fish & Wildlife Form 3-177.

faqs.question: How many live animals does the U.S. import?
faqs.answer: $3.71B of live animals in 2025, of which $2.14B was cattle. Canada supplied 70% of the total; Mexico, still the No. 2 source, fell from $1.31B to $329M as its cattle shipments dropped.

seo.title: Tariffs on U.S. Live Animal Exports by Country — HTS Chapter 01 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Which countries buy U.S. live animals ($1.68B in 2025), the tariff each charges on U.S.-origin cattle, horses and poultry, and every tariff change since January 2025.

usExports.intro: The rest of this report looks at what the U.S. charges on live animals coming **in**. This page looks the other way: the countries that **buy** U.S. live animals, the tariff each one charges on U.S.-origin goods, and the tariff actions between the U.S. and that country since January 2025. Rates are shown for the products each country mainly buys, not every tariff line.
usExports.valueBasis: FOB value of U.S. exports, as reported by the United States to UN Comtrade

markets.headline: U.S. cattle and horses entered Canada duty-free throughout. Neither the 2025 nor the 2026 Canadian counter-tariffs reached them; only three over-quota poultry lines were briefly hit in 2025.

updates.title: Counter-tariffs on 629 U.S. products (answering U.S. Section 338 tariffs)
updates.detail: Mostly steel, aluminum, dairy and machinery; the list starts at dairy (0402) and has no Chapter 01 lines. Applies even to CUSMA-qualifying goods.

updates.title: Most 2025 counter-tariffs removed
updates.detail: Canada repealed the March 2025 surtax on consumer and farm goods; only its steel, aluminum and auto surtaxes stayed.

updates.title: 25% counter-tariff on C$30B of U.S. goods
updates.detail: Covered three over-quota live poultry lines (0105.11.22, 0105.94.92, 0105.99.12) that already carry 154–238% over-quota duties. No cattle, horse or swine lines. In-quota U.S. poultry stayed free under CUSMA.

markets.headline: No Mexican tariff change has touched U.S. live animals; they still enter free under USMCA, which continues under annual reviews after the July 2026 joint review.

updates.title: USMCA joint review: U.S. declines to extend, annual reviews begin
updates.detail: Preferences continue for now; the agreement is reviewed every year instead of being renewed for 16 years. A future exit would expose U.S. goods to Mexican MFN rates.

updates.title: Announced retaliation against U.S. tariffs never applied
updates.detail: Mexico announced countermeasures in March 2025 but never published a list. Its January 2026 tariff increases on non-FTA countries do not apply to U.S. goods.

markets.headline: U.S. horses (mostly thoroughbreds) enter Japan duty-free, and nothing changed in 2025–26.

updates.title: U.S.–Japan agreement
updates.detail: Japan committed to buy more U.S. rice, corn and soybeans (about $8B a year). No change to Japanese Chapter 01 tariffs, and Japan did not retaliate.

markets.headline: Pure-bred breeding horses enter the EU free; other horses pay the 11.5% EU tariff. The EU’s retaliation list included non-breeding horses but was never applied.

updates.title: EU–U.S. framework tariff cuts adopted
updates.detail: Cuts EU tariffs on U.S. industrial goods to zero plus some farm goods and quotas; the farm annexes start at Chapter 07, so live animals are unchanged.

updates.title: EU countermeasures on about €93B of U.S. goods
updates.detail: The list included non-breeding horses, cattle, swine, sheep and some poultry, but not pure-bred breeding horses. Suspended in August 2025 and repeatedly since.

markets.headline: U.S. breeding chicks already enter duty-free. The signed U.S.–Indonesia trade agreement would zero the remaining 5% lines but is not yet in force; the growth in 2025 came from Indonesia’s bigger breeding-stock quota.

updates.title: U.S.–Indonesia Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed
updates.detail: Indonesia would remove tariffs on over 99% of U.S. lines and committed to buy about 580,000 U.S. grandparent-stock birds. It takes effect 90 days after both sides finish legal procedures; Indonesia’s parliament has not ratified it yet.

updates.title: Breeding-stock import quota raised to 800,000 birds
updates.detail: Not a tariff: Indonesia’s grandparent-stock broiler import quota rose from 578,000 (2025) to 800,000 birds (2026).

markets.headline: Breeding chicks enter at 0%. Thailand pledged to remove tariffs on about 99% of U.S. goods, but the agreement is not signed yet.

updates.title: U.S.–Thailand reciprocal trade framework
updates.detail: Would cut the 40% lines on non-breeding live animals. The Thai prime minister said on Oct 7, 2026 that talks were close to completion.

markets.headline: Registered breeding horses enter free; other horses pay 10%. The 2025 U.S.–UK deal did not change live-animal tariffs, so the 2025 drop is not tariff-driven.

updates.title: U.S.–UK Economic Prosperity Deal
updates.detail: UK concessions were a beef quota and a duty-free ethanol quota; no change to UK tariffs on live animals.

markets.headline: U.S. breeding chicks enter duty-free. State-level bird-flu bans and their lifting drive the swings, not tariffs.

updates.title: Bird-flu bans lifted on Illinois and Wisconsin
updates.detail: Not a tariff: the Philippines bans poultry from U.S. states with outbreaks and lifts bans as states recover.

updates.title: U.S.–Philippines reciprocal trade deal announced
updates.detail: Philippine concessions announced so far cover autos, soy, wheat and pharmaceuticals; nothing on live animals.

markets.headline: U.S. horses face little or no duty. Saudi Arabia raised duties on live poultry and pure-bred breeding cattle in June 2026 — the only Chapter 01 tariff increase among these buyers apart from China. U.S. cattle sales there fell to almost zero in 2025, before that change.

updates.title: Customs duty increases on 51 farm and food lines
updates.now: 15% live poultry · 5% breeding cattle · 7% breeding sheep/goats
updates.detail: Applies to all origins, not only the U.S. Horses are not on the list.

markets.headline: U.S. breeding chicks briefly faced an extra 125% in April 2025 and still pay an extra 10%. Bird-flu restrictions and China’s switch to domestic breeds best explain the fall from $58.6M to $9.1M.

updates.title: U.S.–China Board of Trade product lists
updates.detail: China’s list of U.S. goods whose tariffs would return to MFN reportedly includes horses, donkeys and mules; poultry is not mentioned.

updates.title: Extra 10–15% tariffs on U.S. farm goods removed
updates.detail: The March 2025 farm-goods list (chicken meat, pork, beef, grains, …) had no Chapter 01 lines.

updates.title: Extra tariff on all U.S. goods cut to 10%
updates.status: In force; truce extended to Jan 10, 2027
updates.detail: Rose 34% → 84% → 125% in April 2025, then cut to 10% with 24 points suspended. Applies to live animals on top of China’s normal rate.

updates.title: Bird-flu restrictions lifted for 17 U.S. states
updates.detail: Not a tariff. Whether breeding stock is covered is unconfirmed.

usExports.why:
The U.S. imports far more live animals than it exports ($3.71B vs $1.68B in 2025), and Canada is both its biggest supplier and its biggest buyer. That is not a contradiction — the two directions are different animals at different stages of the supply chain:

- **Pigs only go south.** Canada sent about $633M of swine to the U.S. in 2025, mostly young pigs finished in Midwest barns; the U.S. sold Canada under $1M.
- **Cattle cross both ways.** Canada sends feeder and slaughter cattle to U.S. feedlots and packing plants (about $1.8B), while U.S. cattle ($784M) go north to Canadian feedlots and packers — driven by local feed costs, plant capacity, the season and how close a ranch is to the border.
- **Genetics go out.** U.S. exports are dominated by breeding stock: day-old broiler breeder chicks to Mexico, Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines, and thoroughbred and sport horses to Japan, Ireland, the UK and Saudi Arabia.

So what a country pays for U.S. animals depends on the product: breeding stock is duty-free almost everywhere, while animals for fattening or slaughter often carry tariffs.
